checks.claim: Key: waves arriving twice as long (z = 1) mean the distances between galaxies have doubled since the light set out (1 + z = a(now)/a(then))
checks.note: Grokipedia gives 1 + z = a(t0)/a(te) and says the wavelength is stretched by the factor by which space has expanded. 'Distances between galaxies' means unbound ones; fine at this level.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the galaxy races through space at twice light's speed
checks.note: The expansion is of space itself; no object travels faster than c through local space. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the light slowed to half its speed (and context: light's speed in empty space never changes)
Wrong choice and context: dust reddens a galaxy's colour by taking out more blue than red light but cannot move the lines
checks.note: Grokipedia: dust reddening 'tilts the continuum spectrum redward without shifting emission lines'.

checks.claim: Stem: red shift is measured from the lines in a galaxy's spectrum, each marking one exact colour
checks.note: Galaxy spectra carry absorption and emission lines; either kind is used. Naming only the dark lines is a fair simplification.

checks.claim: Context: the universe was then half its present size; nothing travels through space faster than light
checks.note: Half the scale factor; standard plain-words phrasing.

checks.claim: Alpher and Herman, 1948, predicted the relic glow at about 5 K, building on Gamow's hot early universe
checks.note: Wikipedia: first predicted in 1948 by Alpher and Herman 'in a correction they prepared for a paper by' Gamow, 'down to a temperature of about 5 K'. Grokipedia CMB: about 5 K in their 1948 and 1949 publications, building on Gamow's work. Wikipedia's Alpher page calls the theory 'Alpher and Gamow's'; 'George Gamow's theory' for the hot dense young universe is a fair simplification.

checks.claim: Penzias and Wilson picked up the glow in 1964
checks.note: First clear measurement 20 May 1964; published 1965.

checks.claim: Key: the theory had foretold the glow before it was found
checks.note: The steady state expected no uniform relic radiation; the 1948 forecast came first.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: its warmth matched the 1948 figure to the degree
checks.note: Penzias and Wilson's excess was 3.5 +/- 1.0 K; today 2.7255 K; the forecast was 5 K. Not a match to the degree.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it was the first sign that the universe expands (context: the expansion shown since 1929)
checks.note: Hubble's law established in 1929.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: its finders built their horn to hunt for it (context: a horn built for satellite signals; they were not looking for the glow)
checks.note: Built 1959 by Bell Labs engineers for NASA's Project Echo; Penzias and Wilson used it to measure Milky Way radio emission, 'without prior intent to search for cosmological signals'.

checks.claim: Context: Alpher and Herman's forecast drew almost no notice
checks.note: 'More or less forgotten until they were rediscovered by Robert Dicke and Yakov Zel'dovich in the early 1960s'.

checks.claim: Context: the glow came out at about 3 degrees (2.725 today)
Hoyle and his allies, who never accepted the Big Bang, proposed the glow was starlight absorbed and re-emitted by dust
checks.note: Grokipedia CMB: in the late 1960s and 1970s Hoyle and collaborators proposed 'thermalization of starlight by intergalactic metallic dust'. Grokipedia Fred Hoyle: he defended steady-state variants into the late 1990s (he died in 2001). Wikipedia Steady-state model: light from ancient stars 'scattered by galactic dust'.

checks.claim: COBE launched in 1989; Mather's FIRAS found a near-perfect blackbody, 2.725 K, deviations under 50 parts per million
checks.note: Launched 18 November 1989; 2.725 +/- 0.002 K; 'deviations less than 50 parts per million'; the spectral result 'ruled out alternative theories such as the steady-state model'.

checks.claim: Key: dust at many temperatures would blend many curves, so it could not give one pure blackbody
checks.note: Wikipedia: the spectrum 'could hardly be formed by the superposition of contributions from a multitude of dust clumps at different temperatures as well as at different redshifts'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: dust gives off no light at the glow's wavelengths (context: dust glows smoothly at these wavelengths)
checks.note: Galactic thermal dust is the main foreground in Planck's CMB channels (100-857 GHz) and was subtracted from COBE FIRAS maps (Grokipedia COBE). Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: dust would glow in bright lines, not a smooth curve
checks.note: Dust thermal emission 'follows a modified blackbody spectrum', a continuum.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: starlight passes through dust without warming it (context: dust warms to 10-100 K)
checks.note: Grains absorb starlight and re-emit it thermally; temperatures 'generally fall between 10 and 100 K'.

checks.claim: Context: the Big Bang explains the pure curve as light once in balance with the hot, dense young gas
Smoot's team, another COBE instrument (DMR), reported in April 1992 spots warmer or cooler by about one part in 100,000
checks.note: Announced 23 April 1992 at the APS April Meeting in Washington; Grokipedia COBE: about 30 microkelvins on 7-10 degree scales, about 1 part in 100,000 of 2.725 K.

checks.claim: Theorists had predicted the ripples; astronomers had hunted for them for 27 years
checks.note: LBL, 1 May 1992: 'had been predicted by theorists but, up until now, never had been detected'; 'Scientists have searched for these irregularities for 27 years'.

checks.claim: Key: galaxies had to grow from slightly denser patches
checks.note: Fluctuations of 1 part in 100,000 'represent the seeds of large-scale structure formation'; LBL: 'the primordial seeds that grew into present-day galaxies and clusters of galaxies'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: the Big Bang's starting spot stays warmest; starlight warms it where galaxies are thickest; separate sources give it off
checks.note: No centre to the expansion; the glow set out about 380,000 years after the beginning, long before stars; it is far too even for separate sources. None is a reason theorists expected ripples.

checks.claim: Context: glow released about 380,000 years after the beginning, long before the first stars
checks.note: About 380,000 years, at about 3000 K.

checks.claim: Context: Mather and Smoot shared the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for the glow's curve and its ripples
checks.note: Citation: 'for their discovery of the blackbody form and anisotropy of the cosmic microwave background radiation'.

checks.claim: The first minutes predict about three-quarters hydrogen and one-quarter helium by mass
checks.note: About 75% hydrogen; predicted Yp = 0.247.

checks.claim: Tested in glowing gas clouds of small galaxies poor in elements heavier than helium
checks.note: Yp 'is inferred from helium emission lines in extragalactic H II regions ... in low-metallicity galaxies', extrapolated to zero metallicity.

checks.claim: Key: stars have added the least helium to them
checks.note: Stars produce helium, so measurements need correction for stellar processing; the least-processed gas is closest to primordial.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: nearest the Big Bang's spot; heavy elements hide helium's light; helium leaks away over time
checks.note: No centre; metal-poor regions are chosen for stellar enrichment, not because metals hide helium lines; helium does not 'leak away'. None defensible.

checks.claim: Context: helium near 24.5 percent by mass, close to the prediction
checks.note: PDG 2024 Yp = 0.245 +/- 0.003, within about 1 sigma of 0.247. A 2025 Subaru/EMPRESS value (0.2387) is lower; 'near 24.5' still stands.

checks.claim: Context: the first minutes made about ten times more helium than all the stars since
checks.note: OpenStax: '10 times more helium was manufactured in the first 4 minutes of the universe' than in all later generations of stars.

checks.claim: Context: Hoyle with Roger Tayler in 1964 argued there is too much helium for the stars to have made
checks.note: Hoyle and Tayler, 'The Mystery of the Cosmic Helium Abundance', Nature 203, 1108 (1964): made the case for a large primordial helium abundance stars could not simply explain.

checks.claim: WMAP launched 2001; the European Planck satellite after it mapped the ripples more finely; the ripples' strength at each size depends on the universe's contents
checks.note: WMAP launched 30 June 2001 (Grokipedia WMAP); Planck (ESA) built to measure the fluctuations to 'determine the composition and evolution of the universe'.

checks.claim: Key: atoms make up about a twentieth of the universe
checks.note: Planck, 21 March 2013: normal matter 'only about 4.9%'. Later Planck releases keep about 4.9%.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: a quarter, half, nearly all
checks.note: About 27% is dark matter (the 'quarter' is dark matter, not atoms); ordinary matter about 5%.

checks.claim: Context: Planck 2013: 4.9% ordinary, 26.8% dark matter, 68.3% dark energy, age 13.8 billion years; WMAP much the same
checks.note: Age 13.82 billion years. WMAP: about 4.6%, 24%, 71.4%.

checks.claim: Context: neither dark matter nor dark energy has been identified (about 95% of unknown nature)
checks.note: 'Dark matter's composition remains unknown'; no definitive detection as of 2026. Honest open question.

checks.claim: Context: the expansion rate from the glow disagrees with the rate from nearby galaxies
checks.note: Planck 67.4 vs SH0ES 73.0 km/s/Mpc, 5-6 sigma, unresolved as of 2026. Some local methods (CCHP TRGB, about 70) fall between. Told as a puzzle, this is honest; if the tension resolves, the sentence would date.

checks.claim: Stem: every star, planet and gas cloud seen is made of atoms
checks.note: Plain words for ordinary (baryonic) matter, the usual NASA phrasing. Neutron stars and plasma are a pedant's exception; fine at grade 9.

checks.claim: Stem: 'Fritz Zwicky measured in 1933 how fast the galaxies of the Coma Cluster ... move about inside it, from the shifts in their light'
checks.note: Zwicky did not measure the shifts: he used redshifts that Edwin Hubble and Milton Humason had published in 1931. Bertone and Hooper (A History of Dark Matter) say Hubble and Humason had already noticed Coma's large spread of speeds; Zwicky's step was applying the virial theorem. His own paper presents the velocities as a compilation citing Hubble and Humason, ApJ 74, 43 (https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/March17/Zwicky/Zwicky3.html). (Grokipedia's Coma page says 'Zwicky measured redshifts', which the primary source does not support.) FIX: 'Fritz Zwicky worked out in 1933, from the shifts in their light that Edwin Hubble and Milton Humason had measured, how fast the galaxies of the Coma Cluster ... move about inside it.'

checks.claim: Coma Cluster, more than a thousand galaxies
checks.note: 'Over 1,000 confirmed members' (a 2024 catalogue gives 2,157). Zwicky himself counted 800.

checks.claim: Speeds of some 1,000 km/s, far more than visible matter could hold together
checks.note: Zwicky: 'a medium-sized Doppler effect of 1000 km/s or more'; Bertone and Hooper: visible mass predicts about 80 km/s.

checks.claim: Key: far more matter is there than gives off light
checks.note: Zwicky: density 'at least 400 times greater' than luminous matter; 'dark matter exists in much greater density than luminous matter'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: cluster flying apart; gravity pulls harder at vast distances; his speeds too high
checks.note: None was Zwicky's conclusion.

checks.claim: Context: he called it dunkle Materie; overlooked for decades
checks.note: Wikipedia footnote quotes the German 1933 paper's 'dunkle Materie'; Bertone and Hooper find almost no citations 1934-44.

checks.claim: Context: modern studies put dark matter at about nine-tenths of the cluster's mass; what it is remains unknown; a few physicists test modified gravity
checks.note: Coma: dark matter 'about 90%' (80-90%), hot gas about 10%. MOND alters gravity at low accelerations (Grokipedia Dark matter). Honest open question.

checks.claim: Context: 'keeping their speed means the pull keeps growing outward'
checks.note: Wrong physics. For a flat rotation curve the MASS enclosed grows in step with radius (Grokipedia: 'the enclosed mass continues to increase linearly with radius'). The pull itself (v squared over r) gets weaker outward, just more slowly than if the mass sat in the centre. FIX: 'keeping their speed means the mass inside their orbits keeps growing outward, so the galaxy must sit in a vast halo of unseen matter...'

checks.claim: Stem: Rubin and Ford 'measured how fast stars and glowing gas circle the centre of the Andromeda Galaxy', reported 1970
checks.note: Minor. The 1970 paper ('Rotation of the Andromeda Nebula from a Spectroscopic Survey of Emission Regions', ApJ 159, 379) measured glowing gas only: 67 H II regions 3 to 24 kpc out, mostly from H-alpha, plus an [N II] gas line in the nucleus. No stars. FIX: 'measured how fast glowing clouds of gas circle the centre of the Andromeda Galaxy, out to its faint edges, and reported in 1970.' Year, names and Ford's spectrograph are right.

checks.claim: Stem: the Sun holds almost all the Solar System's mass; Neptune circles far more slowly than Mercury
checks.note: Mercury 47.4 km/s, Neptune 5.4 km/s; the Sun about 99.86% of the mass (Grokipedia Solar System).

checks.claim: Stem: in Andromeda the outer parts circle about as fast as the inner ones
checks.note: 'The outermost components of the galaxy were moving as quickly as those close to the center.'

checks.claim: Key: much of the mass lies far out, where little light shines
checks.note: Flat curves imply mass growing with radius beyond the light. Rubin and Ford did not claim dark matter in 1970, but the stem asks what the result shows, so the key stands.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: nearly all in the bright centre; most in a central black hole; less mass than starlight suggests
checks.note: Each would make the outer speeds fall off as in Keplerian orbits.

checks.claim: Context: halo five to ten times the visible mass; 21 spirals in a 1980 study; Rubin did not rule out alternatives; no particle detected
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'at least five to ten times more mass than can be observed directly' and 'Rubin did not rule out alternative models'. Rubin, Ford and Thonnard 1980, ApJ 238, 471, 'Rotational properties of 21 Sc galaxies'. Grokipedia Dark matter: no definitive detection as of 2026.

checks.claim: Context: 'Fainter meant farther, so space had stretched more since the light set out than a slowing expansion allows'
checks.note: Wrong physics, and it contradicts this unit's own first question. How much space has stretched since the light set out IS the measured red shift (1 + z), so it is the same in both models. Being fainter than expected for that red shift means farther, so the light took longer to be stretched that much. The expansion was slower in the past and has sped up since. FIX: 'Fainter meant farther: at the same red shift, the light had been travelling longer than a slowing expansion allows, so the universe grew more slowly long ago than it does now: the expansion has been speeding up for the last 5 or 6 billion years.'

checks.claim: Stem: a Type Ia supernova peaks at nearly the same brightness every time, so its apparent brightness gives its distance
checks.note: Strictly 'standardizable' (corrected for how fast each fades); 'nearly the same' is a fair grade-9 simplification.

checks.claim: Perlmutter's team and a rival team with Schmidt and Riess, expecting deceleration, found distant supernovae fainter than expected in 1998
checks.note: Supernova Cosmology Project (Perlmutter); High-Z team (Schmidt, Riess); 'fainter than expected in a decelerating universe'.

checks.claim: Key: the expansion has been speeding up
checks.note: Acceleration began about 5-6 billion years ago.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: slowing even faster; dust dimmed them; such stars exploded more dimly long ago
checks.note: Dust is corrected for by its reddening; no strong evidence of supernova evolution at z < 1. Neither was the teams' conclusion.

checks.claim: Context: corroborated by galaxy maps and the background glow; 2011 Nobel shared by Perlmutter, Schmidt and Riess; cause named dark energy, nature unknown
checks.note: BAO and Planck corroborate; Nobel 2011 (half Perlmutter, half Schmidt and Riess: 'shared' is right). Dark energy's nature unknown (NASA: 'We don't know'). Honest open question.

unit_notes: Six ok, three errors, none uncertain. All three errors are cheap wording fixes. (1) Zwicky used Hubble and Humason's 1931 redshifts; he did not measure them. (2) Rubin's context says the 'pull keeps growing outward': it is the enclosed mass that grows. Her 1970 Andromeda survey measured gas (H II regions), not stars. (3) The supernova context says space 'stretched more' since emission, but the stretch is the measured red shift. The distance is what came out larger. Open questions are told honestly throughout: dark matter (no particle found as of 2026, MOND mentioned), dark energy (unknown) and the Hubble tension (unresolved as of 2026; that sentence could date). Spot-checked and right: Alpher and Herman 5 K (1948), the Holmdel horn's Echo purpose, COBE 1989 / FIRAS 50 ppm / DMR 23 April 1992 / 2006 Nobel, the LBL '27 years' line, Yp 0.245 (PDG 2024), Planck 2013 at 4.9 / 26.8 / 68.3, and Hoyle and Tayler 1964.
